Li.summary: Evidence for Bose-Einstein condensation of a gas of spin-polarised 7Li atoms, reported in a Physical Review Letters abstract published 28 August 1995.

citations.title: Evidence of Bose-Einstein Condensation in an Atomic Gas with Attractive Interactions

Cr.summary: Bose-Einstein condensation of chromium, with the isotope 52Cr named in the abstract, published 29 April 2005.

citations.title: Bose-Einstein Condensation of Chromium
citations.locator: Abstract, first sentence; 52Cr named in the abstract; published 29 April 2005

Sr.summary: Two strontium isotopes have Bose-Einstein condensates: 84Sr (first realised 2009) and 88Sr (first realised 2010, by sympathetic cooling with 87Sr).

citations.title: Bose-Einstein Condensation of Strontium
citations.locator: Abstract, first sentence; isotope 84Sr named in the abstract; published 9 November 2009

citations.title: Bose-Einstein condensation of 88Sr through sympathetic cooling with 87Sr

citations.locator: Abstract, first sentence; 164Dy named later in the abstract; published 31 October 2011

Dy.summary: Bose-Einstein condensation of dysprosium, the most magnetic element, with the condensed isotope 164Dy named in the 2011 APS abstract.

Er.summary: Bose-Einstein condensation of erbium-168, reported in the 2012 APS abstract as pure condensates of up to 7 x 10^4 atoms.

H.summary: NASA states that the first generation of stars (Population III) were made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, so hydrogen was a main part of them. This is a statement about the first stars, not about every star.

citations.title: First Stars: Composition - NASA Science
citations.locator: Main text, first generation of stars
citations.quote: The first generation of stars, also known as Population III stars, were made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium.

He.summary: NASA states that the first generation of stars (Population III) were made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, so helium was a main part of them. This is a statement about the first stars, not about every star.

citations.title: First Stars: Composition - NASA Science
citations.locator: Main text, first generation of stars
citations.quote: The first generation of stars, also known as Population III stars, were made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium.

Ne.summary: NIST describes neon gas as giving an orange-red light when an electric charge is applied, and states that gases release a specific, characteristic wavelength of photons, which sets the colour.

citations.title: Luminous Script Signs: The Origins of the 'Neon Sign' - NIST
citations.locator: Colour statement for neon; statement on characteristic wavelengths
citations.quote: Neon gas produces an orange-red color.

Ar.summary: NIST describes argon gas as giving a blue light when an electric charge is applied.

citations.title: Luminous Script Signs: The Origins of the 'Neon Sign' - NIST
citations.quote: This gas produces a blue color.

N.summary: Nitrogen gas in the upper atmosphere produces auroras. Energetic particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms at about 100 to 400 km altitude; NOAA's National Calibration Center lists nitrogen's aurora colours as blue and purple.

citations.title: NOAA National Calibration Center - Aurora
citations.locator: Aurora mechanism and colour list (Oxygen: green and red, Nitrogen: blue and purple)
citations.quote: Particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere (~100-400 km altitude)

O.summary: NASA states that oxygen in auroras can produce green and red light.

citations.title: Auroras - NASA Science
citations.quote: Oxygen excited to different energy levels can produce green and red.
